about.title: Tang and Song China and the Islamic Golden Age
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are 31 short steps, and most end with a quick check. Two civilizations plus a debate put this near the top of a half-hour class. Anyone who wants a shorter class can stop after step 25 and read the debate steps later.

say.text: Welcome. Today we visit two great centers of science, trade and invention: China under the Tang and Song dynasties, and Baghdad under the Abbasid caliphs.

show.text: Two Great Centers: Tang–Song China and Abbasid Baghdad

say.text: First, a map of time. The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907. The Song followed, from 960 to 1279. Baghdad's House of Wisdom is traditionally dated to about 830.

show.text: 618–907 Tang | 960–1279 Song | about 830 House of Wisdom, Baghdad

say.text: People call these centuries 'golden ages'. A golden age is a time when art, learning and wealth all bloom together. Hold that phrase. At the end we will ask if it fits.

show.text: Golden age

ask.right: A time when art, learning and wealth all bloom together
wrong: A time when everything was made of gold
A war that lasted a hundred years
A time when nobody made mistakes
ask.why: A golden age is a way of describing a flourishing time. It is not about real gold.

say.text: Start with Tang China. Its capital, Chang'an, is today's Xi'an. It sat on the Silk Road, the chain of trade routes joining China to lands in the west.

show.text: China's capital Chang'an (modern Xi'an) at the eastern end of the Silk Road, with routes running west across Central Asia

say.text: Ideas travelled with traders. In 635 a Christian named Alopun reached Chang'an. Emperor Taizong approved his preaching and ordered a church built there.

show.text: A Tang street scene in Chang'an: merchants in many styles of dress, camels, and a small church beside Buddhist temples

ask.q: What does Alopun's visit show about Tang Chang'an?
ask.right: People from other lands and faiths were welcomed there
wrong: Only Buddhists were allowed to live there
ask.why: The emperor allowed Alopun to preach and ordered a church built. That shows an open, mixed city.

say.text: The Tang is also famous for poetry. About 48,900 poems survive, by some 2,200 poets. Li Bai and Du Fu are the best known.

show.text: 48,900 Tang poems still survive

say.text: Now the first invention: printing. Before it, every book was copied by hand. That was slow, and it let mistakes creep in.

show.text: Printing

say.text: In the Tang, carvers began block printing. They carved a whole page into a wooden board, inked it, and pressed paper onto it. One board could make many copies.

show.text: A carver cutting Chinese characters into a wooden board, with a stack of printed pages beside him

ask.q: Why did copying books by hand limit how many books existed?
ask.right: It was slow and mistakes crept in
wrong: Books had to be written in secret
ask.why: Hand copying took a lot of time and effort and often added errors. Block printing made copies faster.

say.text: Here is proof. The Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scroll, is dated 11 May 868. It is the earliest dated printed book known.

ask.q: In what year was the Diamond Sutra printed?
ask.why: Its printed date is 11 May 868, in the Tang dynasty. That makes it the earliest dated printed book known.

say.text: A man named Wang Jie had it made, to give away free in honor of his parents. It lay sealed in a cave at Dunhuang until about 1900. Today it is in the British Library.

show.text: A long woodblock-printed paper scroll with a carved picture of the Buddha teaching at the start

say.text: The Song dynasty improved on this. Around 1040 an official named Bi Sheng made single characters that could be rearranged and reused. That is movable type.

show.text: Movable type

say.text: His first characters were made of fragile clay or porcelain. Chinese uses thousands of characters, so carving them was hard work.

show.text: Small clay blocks, each with one carved character, arranged in rows on an iron plate

ask.q: What was new about movable type?
ask.right: Single characters could be rearranged and reused
wrong: A whole page was carved into one board
ask.why: Block printing carves a whole page. Movable type uses single characters that can be reused for new pages.

say.text: Why did printing matter? The Song government promoted printing of the Confucian texts that exam candidates had to study. Printing also helped literacy grow.

show.text: Printed Confucian texts for exams | More readers | A larger learned class

say.text: Second invention: gunpowder. It was first developed in the Tang. One account says it grew out of alchemy, early experiments with substances. It was used for fireworks, and later for weapons.

show.text: Gunpowder

ask.q: In which dynasty was gunpowder first developed?
ask.why: Gunpowder was first developed in the Tang. The Song then built many weapons with it.

say.text: Song soldiers used 'flying fire' arrows, grenades, flamethrowers and landmines. In 1279 the Mongols ended the Song and used gunpowder weapons against them.

show.text: Flying fire arrows | Grenades | Flamethrowers | Landmines

say.text: Third invention: the compass. At first it was a south-pointing spoon of lodestone, a naturally magnetic rock. It dates back to the Han dynasty and was used for divination.

show.text: Compass

ask.q: What were the earliest compasses used for?
ask.why: The early 'spoon' compass was used for divination. Navigation came later.

say.text: In 1088 the Song scholar Shen Kuo wrote the first known description of the magnetic needle compass. A book by Zhu Yu in 1119 outlined its use for sailing at sea.

show.text: 1088 Shen Kuo describes the needle compass | 1119 Zhu Yu describes use at sea

ask.q: Who wrote the first known description of the magnetic needle compass?
ask.why: Shen Kuo described it in 1088. Zhu Yu's 1119 book was the first to outline its use at sea.

say.text: In Europe the first description of the compass came from Alexander Neckam in 1187. That was about 99 years after Shen Kuo's.
Song China was an age of invention. It gave us printing, paper money, porcelain, tea, restaurants, gunpowder and the compass. Thinkers like Shen Kuo and Su Song also pushed early science forward.

show.text: Printing | Paper money | Porcelain | Tea | Restaurants | Gunpowder | Compass

say.text: Now we travel west to Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid caliphs. They kept a royal library there called the House of Wisdom, with a translation center. One account says it was founded in 830 by al-Ma'mun.

show.text: Baghdad on the Tigris river, west of Persia and east of the Mediterranean

say.text: To translate is to carry a text from one language into another. Scholars in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian and Syriac works into Arabic.

show.text: Translation movement

say.text: The translators were a mixed group. Hunayn ibn Ishaq, who lived from 809 to 873, was a Syrian Christian and the leading translator of the 9th century.

show.text: A scholar at a desk surrounded by scrolls, copying a Greek text into Arabic

ask.q: What did the translators in Baghdad do?
ask.right: They carried works from Greek, Persian and Syriac into Arabic
wrong: They turned Arabic books into Chinese
ask.why: Translation means moving a text from one language to another. In Baghdad that mostly meant translating into Arabic.

say.text: Next, algebra. It means solving for an unknown number by keeping both sides balanced. Try 5 + x = 12. Take 5 away from both sides and you get x = 7.

show.text: Algebra: keep both sides balanced

ask.q: In 5 + x = 12, what do you do to find x?
ask.right: Take 5 away from both sides, so x = 7
ask.why: Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Taking 5 from both sides leaves x = 7.

say.text: Around 830, al-Khwarizmi wrote a famous book in Baghdad: 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'.

show.text: A page of Arabic writing with diagrams of squares and rectangles used to solve equations

say.text: The Arabic word 'al-jabr' in that title, meaning 'completion', became our word 'algebra'. His own name gave us 'algorithm'. His books also helped bring Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe.

show.text: al-jabr → algebra | al-Khwarizmi → algorithm

ask.q: Which English word comes from al-Khwarizmi's name?
ask.why: 'Algorithm' comes from a Latin form of his name. 'Algebra' comes from the title of his book.

say.text: His book was practical. He said it was for everyday needs like inheritance, lawsuits, trade, surveying and digging canals.

show.text: Inheritance | Lawsuits | Trade | Surveying | Canals

say.text: Next, optics, the study of light and sight. An old question: do we see because rays shoot out of our eyes, or because light comes into them?

show.text: Optics

say.text: Both ideas had been proposed before. Ibn al-Haytham argued that light from objects travels in straight lines into our eyes. He tested this with experiments.

show.text: Light rays running in straight lines from a candle through a small hole and into an eye

ask.q: According to Ibn al-Haytham, how do we see?
ask.right: Light from objects travels into our eyes
wrong: Rays shoot out of our eyes
ask.why: He argued that light from objects enters the eye in straight lines, and he backed this with experiments.

say.text: He studied lenses and built apparatus. He tried flat, curved, concave and convex mirrors. His 'Book of Optics' had seven volumes. Sources give different dates for it, from about 1011 to about 1027.

show.text: The Book of Optics: seven volumes

ask.q: How many volumes did the Book of Optics have?
ask.why: The Book of Optics ran to seven volumes.

say.text: Now medicine. Ibn Sina, called Avicenna in Europe, finished The Canon of Medicine in 1025. It was an encyclopedia of medicine in five books, and it stayed an authority for centuries.

show.text: The Canon of Medicine: five books

ask.q: In how many books was The Canon of Medicine arranged?
ask.why: The Canon is an encyclopedia of medicine in five books.

say.text: Cities like Baghdad, Cairo and Harran had famous hospitals. They were called 'bimaristans', from a Persian word meaning 'house of the sick'.

show.text: Bimaristan: house of the sick

say.text: Some were teaching hospitals, where students learned to treat patients. People did not always have to pay.

show.text: A hospital ward with beds, a physician examining a patient, and students watching

ask.right: House of the sick, meaning a hospital
ask.why: It comes from a Persian word meaning 'house of the sick', which is how medieval hospitals were named.

say.text: Let us put the two centers side by side.

show.text: Tang–Song China: block printing, movable type, gunpowder, compass, paper money | Abbasid Baghdad: translation movement, algebra, optics, the Canon of Medicine, bimaristans

say.text: Now the big question. How much of this was new, and how much was borrowed or shared? Start with Baghdad. A Sanskrit astronomy text was translated into Arabic after 770, and Arab scholars adopted the sine function from Indian geometry.

show.text: Debate: how golden, how borrowed?

ask.q: Where did Arab astronomers get the sine function?
wrong: They invented it with no earlier source
ask.why: One source says Arab scholars adopted the sine function from Indian geometry, in place of the Greek method using chords of arcs.

say.text: China built on earlier ideas too. The compass began as a Han-dynasty spoon, and gunpowder began in the Tang. Even the earliest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, carries an Indian Buddhist text that was translated into Chinese about AD 400.

show.text: Compass: Han spoon | Gunpowder: Tang alchemy | Diamond Sutra: Indian text, translated into Chinese about 400

say.text: Even the House of Wisdom is debated. Britannica says scholarship did flourish in Baghdad, but there is little evidence the House of Wisdom was at the center of it.

show.text: Little evidence that the House of Wisdom was at the center of Baghdad's scholarship (Britannica)

say.text: The scholar Dimitri Gutas argued that its main job was housing Persian-to-Arabic translation. He said the Greek translation movement was separate. Historians still agree Baghdad had a rich library and scholarly culture.

show.text: Idea one: a grand academy for all translation | Idea two: a royal library with a narrower role

ask.q: What do some historians say about the House of Wisdom?
ask.right: It existed, but it may not have been the center of all Baghdad's translation
ask.why: The debate is over how big, formal and central it was. It is not about whether it existed.

say.text: How did the Chinese inventions travel west? One account says Arab traders carried them. Another says they spread along Mongol trade networks. Both agree they reached the Islamic world and Europe.

show.text: Account one: Arab traders | Account two: Mongol trade networks

say.text: So was it a golden age? Scholars still argue over its roots: some stress Arab-Islamic thinkers, others stress Greek, Persian and Indian traditions. A fair summary is that both centers built on earlier ideas from many places, and both added new work.

show.text: Built on others, then added their own

ask.right: Both centers built on earlier ideas from many places and added important new work
wrong: Nothing from either place ever reached Europe
ask.why: Each center borrowed and shared ideas, and each also added its own advances. The inventions and books we met today show both.

say.text: To recap: China gave us printing, gunpowder and the compass. Baghdad gave us algebra, optics and the Canon of Medicine. Next class we visit Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia and medieval India.

show.text: Printing | Gunpowder | Compass | Algebra | Optics | Medicine | Next: Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia and medieval India

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: China was under the Tang dynasty. In Baghdad, Harun al-Rashid exchanged envoys with Charlemagne, who was crowned emperor in Rome on 25 December 800. The caliph sent him a white elephant named Abul-Abbas.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote his algebra in Baghdad around 830. In Tang China the Diamond Sutra was printed on 11 May 868. That was about four decades later.

Ibn Sina finished the Canon of Medicine in 1025. Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics was written in the early 1000s, with dates given from about 1011 to 1027. Su Song was born in 1020, Shen Kuo in 1031, and Bi Sheng made movable type around 1040.
Shen Kuo described the magnetic needle compass in 1088. Alexander Neckam gave Europe's first description in 1187.
1258 marked the end of Baghdad's House of Wisdom as an institution. In 1279 the Mongols overthrew the Song.

other_side.claim: The House of Wisdom was the great academy of Baghdad and the heart of the translation movement.
other_side.other_view: Britannica says scholarship flourished but there is little evidence the House of Wisdom was central to it. Dimitri Gutas argued its main function was housing Persian-to-Arabic translation, and that Greek translation was separate. Some historians say the 'academy' picture was built in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Other sources say the real debate is about how big, formal and central it was, not whether it existed.

other_side.claim: The Islamic Golden Age was a brilliant, original burst of new knowledge.
other_side.other_view: Scholars debate its roots. Some stress Arab-Islamic thinkers. Others stress Greek, Persian and Indian traditions that were already in the region, and Arabic science took in Indian astronomy and the sine function. A fair reading is that scholars built on shared knowledge and added new work.
His book is a landmark in systematic treatment of equations. But it cites no earlier authors, so historians infer from the text what he drew on. They argue over how much came from earlier work.

other_side.claim: Ibn al-Haytham was first to show that we see because light enters the eye.
other_side.other_view: Sources say both theories of vision, light entering the eye and rays leaving it, had been put forward before him. His novelty was systematic experiment. Dates for the Book of Optics also vary between sources.

other_side.claim: Song China invented the compass, gunpowder and printing.
other_side.other_view: The Song made major breakthroughs, but roots go back earlier: the compass to a Han-era spoon, gunpowder to the Tang, and block printing to the Tang. Shen Kuo's 1088 text described the needle but did not specifically outline sea use. Zhu Yu's 1119 book did.

other_side.claim: Chinese inventions reached the West through Arab traders.
other_side.other_view: One account says Arab traders carried them to Europe. Another says they travelled through Mongol trade networks into the Islamic world and Europe.
